headline: Peanut Bunker Pile Into Oyster Creek — Blues Stay Steady, Fluke Fade at Double Creek
subhead: The bait's building faster than the stripers are willing to commit, but bluefish, blowfish, and the last of the fluke are keeping the fleet busy from Barnegat Light to Tices Shoal.
body_markdown:
Forty years back I was mate on a Point Pleasant boat the first week of September, and the skipper pointed out over the transom at a school of peanut bunker so thick it looked like the water had grown skin. He told me, "Gus, when they pile in like that before the first cold snap, mark the date — the bass show up right behind them, but not till the water tells them it's time." That lesson has held up every September since, and it's exactly what's playing out on Barnegat Bay right now. The bunker are here, thick as I've seen them in years, but the water hasn't given the signal yet.

We're sitting with bay temps still hanging in the low-to-mid 70s, which is plenty warm for stripers to stage on bait without committing to a real blitz. Bunker schools have been thickening up from the mouth of Toms River down through Oyster Creek and into the deeper stretch by Double Creek Channel, and every mate on the dock has a story about bass shadowing those schools without ever breaking the surface. We flagged this exact pattern last week — said the bait needed to concentrate further before the bass would commit in blitz numbers, and that's precisely what's unfolding. The moon builds to full on the 6th and 7th, which is going to tighten that tidal flow and push those bunker schools into tighter, more nervous balls. That's the trigger everybody's waiting on. It just hasn't tripped yet.

Fluke are doing what fluke do this time of year — thinning out of the back bay as the bigger, egg-heavy females start their slide toward the inlet and the ocean-side structure. Double Creek Channel is still giving up keepers, but the numbers are down from where they were in July and August. The better drifts have been on the last two hours of the outgoing, working white Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails right along the channel edges where the current cuts hard against the mud. A few boats working the deeper water off Barnegat Light — down in that 20 to 25 foot range near the inlet rocks — have found a better grade of fish, some pushing 4 and 5 pounds, staged there ahead of their run out through the inlet. If you want fluke this week, fish early and fish the deeper structure. The shallow grass flats that carried the summer bite are mostly picked over now.

Bluefish have been the most dependable thing going, and that's held true basin-wide through the warm water. Snapper blues are thick in the coves and marina basins from Forked River down to Manahawkin, and the adult blues have been chopping up peanut bunker pods around Tices Shoal and along the surf at Island Beach State Park. Small metal — half-ounce Kastmasters and Deadly Dicks — worked fast through the froth has been the ticket, along with poppers on the surface when the blues are actively feeding on top, usually the first hour of light or the last hour before dark. This bite should hold right through Labor Day week as long as the bait stays put, and there's no reason to think it won't.

Blowfish and kingfish are still around on the sandy bottom stretches near Barnegat Light and along the edges of the channel markers south of Waretown, working bloodworm and squid strips on high-low rigs with small hooks. It's a steady, unspectacular bite — good for a family afternoon, not the kind of thing that fills a cooler fast, but reliable if you've got the patience for it.

As for weakfish, the sedges are quiet right now. That's a spring pattern here on Barnegat Bay, and by early September those fish have long since slid out past the inlet or scattered into deeper holes where nobody's really targeting them. If you're chasing weakfish memories, mark your calendar for May and put this week's effort into the bunker-and-blues game instead.

Looking at the next several days, the wind pattern and tide setup favor working the early morning outgoing at Double Creek for what fluke remain, then shifting over to Tices Shoal or the Island Beach surf for blues once the sun gets up and the bait starts moving. The real story to watch is whether we get any kind of overnight cooldown before the weekend. If nighttime temps start dropping even a few degrees, combined with that building moon tightening the bait, this is the week the first real striper activity could break loose inside the bay — probably starting as scattered surface swirls around the bunker schools near Oyster Creek and Toms River before it turns into anything you'd call a blitz. Until that front shows up, the smart play is fishing the edges where bait and current meet, staying mobile, and not wasting a whole tide sitting on water that looked good yesterday but has already emptied out today. The bay's setting up for something — it just hasn't decided to show its hand yet.
